question.problem: Calculate the area of the finite region bounded by the curves $y=-{x}^{2}-2$ and $y=-x-2.$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/af2b16006d5616854a3fb4e5f116c84375ee78f633ab8f313045b3d6feed922b.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-2 & =-x-2 \\ x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(1-x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273827/assets/bf320ce6791c3f776961fee7fe3b7714895a3f5e38d8d721fd653ee816eb8997.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=-x-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=-{x}^{2}-2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(-{x}^{2}-2)-(-x-2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3})-(0-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$
